## If slow isn’t realistic for you

“Slow down” is good advice if you can actually do it. This whole article is mostly about me, but I don’t think this part is unusual.

How fast? It depends a lot on her, I guess. I went years without sex with one girl because she was a virgin. That’s one reason I like virgins: sex is really hard to have unplanned.

If she’s already really into sex, it can be quick. Men naturally love to please women, and it’s hard to break the mood and say, “Hey, sorry, I’m not so keen on sex yet,” when you’re highly turned on yourself. Heat of the moment, etc. Common problem.

So have the deeper conversations by phone or video first, or meet in person around other people. A meetup group, a friend’s event, whatever. Plan not to go home together, and tell her beforehand that you want to keep things less private at first. If you only say it when she asks you to come home, it sounds like rejection.

Islamic culture says a man and woman shouldn’t be alone together before marriage. Conservative Christians say similar things. I don’t accept their solution, but they noticed something real.

If two people are alone, attracted, and turned on, obviously things may happen. We don’t live in tribes anymore either. The people around us usually don’t know both of us, and nobody is there slowing things down while we figure out what this actually is.

Plan for the horny, impulsive person you really are. Before meeting somebody you’re extremely attracted to, masturbate a lot. Then imagine you already had sex with her. How do you feel now? Keep that feeling in mind, especially when you get horny again.

Men should understand they actually do have safe birth-control options that work better than condoms, including Gandarussa herb, and it makes sense to use that. It doesn’t make impulsiveness okay. It just makes pregnancy a bit less likely. Emotional attachment is still just as likely.

If you do have sex quickly, at least don’t let everything else speed up at the same time. Keep socializing with other people together. Try to have some kind of community even if you aren’t in a real one.

Moving in together right away is generally a bad idea. You’re basically getting into common-law marriage without even asking for it. The Bible also says something, I think, about marriage beginning when you sleep in the same tent together.

This is one step that’s easier not to jump into unless you literally can’t pay the rent, because moving isn’t easy. Once you live together, momentum starts making decisions for you.

Formal check-ins help too. Otherwise it’s very easy to assume mind reading, fawn, or idealize how things are. Pick actual dates and ask how the relationship is going before there’s a crisis. Otherwise we’re just riding blind.

Wanting somebody doesn't tell me whether I should have children with her or build a life with her. I can know the first part much faster than the second. A wonderful lover can still be a terrible co-parent, community member, or life partner.

One of the stupid things my brain can do is turn “I'm taking a chance on her” into “she's the right person” after we've been together for a while. Based on what? Sometimes I actually learned something. Sometimes nothing changed except that now I'm attached, and the new certainty is just harder for me to question.

At some point one of you will ask, “Why am I special to you? Why are you with me and not somebody else?” If the answer is basically, “We had sex and got hitched?” I don’t know, that’s a damn shame.

## Not A Performance

When a woman doesn't know how to gently invite a man to lead, she may manufacture a crisis until he is forced to take charge. From the outside, this can look like the result a gentle invitation would have produced. Unfortunately, I've seen a lot of the crisis version. It feels more like drafting somebody into a war than inviting them to a party.

Either person can gently invite the energy they want:

“Honey, how do you see this intuitively?”

or, “Can you help me think through the practical side for a minute?”

That feels much better than, “Do your female/male thing now.”

Nobody should have to prove that energy is their permanent identity. If I have to prove that I’m the man, something has already become fake. Then I have to defend the identity every time I hesitate, cry, need help, or get something wrong.

I don’t actually think of myself as especially masculine. I step into that energy when I see that a woman would appreciate it, and then it comes naturally. Bee once called me her “wife.” I don’t recommend that as a polarity exercise, by the way.

The same is true for a woman. She should not have to perform softness, helplessness, or cuteness every minute to prove she is feminine. Surrender means so much more when she could take control but prefers not to at that moment.

When a strong woman surrenders, she is choosing to, which is sexy. She knows she could drive, but she asks you to drive, because she likes how it feels when you do.

results.text:
# What are you actually choosing together?

A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? It conjures up for me thoughts of romance, sex, exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, spiritual partnership, family identity, or just “we really like each other and we’ll see.” That looseness can be a nice way to flow. It can also let each person imagine a different bundle, then either not label anything or assume one relationship label settled it.

One honest option is basically a "practical partnership." This is very common, especially outside the modern West. Two people may share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, and maybe have sex, without pretending that overwhelming romantic love is what holds it all together.

This feels wrong to me and anyone else who has been in love. Arguably, though, there is nothing inherently wrong with it if both people know what they are choosing. This arrangement has been promoted throughout history because it isn't based on highly fluctuating feelings.

The agreement isn't based on fluctuating feelings, but it doesn't prevent them. One day you may find your heartthrob at work or church or somewhere else, and suddenly wonder why you ever settled for less.

For people who also want romance, another honest option is romance with humility. Even the phrase fights with itself. The love is real. So is the wish to build something, and the bond is serious. The humility is admitting that none of this lets either person guarantee a future feeling.

That admission doesn't prevent exclusivity, shacking up, children, or a life plan. It makes the conversation beforehand more important. What do we do if the romance fades? Maybe we revive it. Maybe we renegotiate the arrangement.

My actual ideal is to have intimacy embedded in community. Obviously, most people are not going to live in a free-love community unless we really have a New Earth soon. But, as Pema Chodron says to prisoners when teaching them meditation, “Start Where You Are.” Build mutual friendships, and keep other sources of meaning and support alive.

Before you commit to one type of relationship, ask each other some real questions:

What are we deciding to join together, and why?

Is this mainly a romance, a practical partnership, or both?

Are we promising actions, or quietly pretending to promise permanent feelings?

If the romance changes, which parts of this agreement still remain?

And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else?

What counts as betrayal, and what just means we need a serious conversation?

Which needs should still be supported mostly outside the relationship?

How should we plan on revisiting this agreement when our lives change?

If we separate, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe any children involved?

These are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with! You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there's real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity.

results.text:
## After leaving

Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided. Saving face is not a reason to hide abuse, coercion, serious deception, or whatever else actually happened. How much you say, who you say it to, and how public you make it should depend on what happened and why you are telling people.

After a breakup, you may see something you genuinely couldn't see while you were bonded. That doesn't automatically mean you're demonizing the other person. It doesn't make your new explanation right either.

Try their perspective. Could they have been internally conflicted? “They were fake all along” can be attractive because it makes everything easier to explain. Don't rule it out if it really is the most parsimonious explanation.

Then ask somebody who isn't heavily invested in your innocence. A therapist, a pastor, or even a stranger can sometimes look at the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend. Even the curiosity can be therapeutic.

Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but it shouldn't be about bypassing your feelings. Pray for your ex's wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and refuse to use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. No, that isn’t true. We partly mirror one another, but each person is also their own unique person, forged from their own influences apart from you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, Devadatta still kept trying to kill him. Looking honestly at your part doesn't erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, "What would Mr. Rogers do?" (if you're old enough to remember that show).

I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn. Doormat mode would be letting them back into your life without making them lose face themselves through a public apology. Allowing an apology is not the same decision as resuming the relationship.

Going back to someone who's already gone through that cycle can be foolish. But realizing they need to apologize publicly for demonizing their ex can really help some people develop honesty.

results.text:
# Tough Love

Romantic love ain't easy, but it is priceless, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable. I can't sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class. (Just kidding, click here!) It's worth every penny if you ask me, but I can’t give you a formula that makes it stay, aside from the obvious 1+1=2.

Making it work takes both people. That's rare, and probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history.

One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with K: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé is coming from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility. They're suspicious of romance. But one of her ideas fits what I’m trying to say: when two people come together, something appears between them that is larger than either person alone. She calls it the spirit of the relationship.

I don’t think that spirit belongs to us. Nobody can command it to remain. At our best, we serve it. We tell the truth, keep doing our own inner play & work (pl/ork), ask the community for help, and listen for what the relationship is becoming. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn't have articulated that since I didn't even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists. But it festers like mold when the environment is perfect for it. The dominant culture seals two people together and calls it privacy. One person is suddenly supposed to be lover, family, community, therapist, and future. Then the culture treats the damage as a purely private failure.

We help make the romantic myths real by acting them out. Jealousy proves love. Feelings can be promised forever. Conflict should stay hidden. If a relationship ends, it failed.
